relations.myth: Old fox couple enters Inari’s service
relations.note: Foxes serve Inari as divine messengers, attendants, and retainers.
Foxes attend Ukanomitama where later shrine theology identifies the grain kami with Inari.
Foxes serve the Inari complex at shrines identifying or jointly worshipping Ukemochi.
Homophonic exegesis reinterpreted the food deity’s name as “three fox kami.”
A white fox serves as Dakiniten’s mount within overlapping Buddhist and Inari traditions.

relations.myth: Fox spirit receives a Buddhist original ground
relations.note: A fox spirit is interpreted through honji-suijaku and assigned Buddhist efficacy.

relations.myth: Kannon intervenes in Buddhist fox narratives
relations.note: Kannon sometimes reveals or heals fox-related affliction and supplies karmic efficacy.
Fox-like izuna familiars serve or accompany this syncretic mountain deity.

relations.myth: Fox spirits undergo Buddhist defeat and pacification
relations.note: Fox spirits are converted, pacified, or interpreted through Buddhist honji-suijaku frameworks.
Late literature identifies Tamamo’s fox with Daji, destroyer of the Shang court.
Late systematization makes Bao Si another identity of the fox later called Tamamo.
